title: Ankush Bahuguna Wore a Pink Suit in London. The Men on the Street Couldn't Handle It.
excerpt: The Indian beauty influencer's viral reel of homophobic taunts on London streets has sparked a diaspora-wide conversation about masculinity, safety, and the myth of Western progressivism.
body:
Ankush Bahuguna thought he knew what to expect from London. The Indian beauty influencer and content creator — known for challenging rigid notions of masculinity through his grooming and fashion content — had visited the city expecting the kind of open-minded progressivism it sells to the world. Instead, what he got was a string of homophobic slurs from men on the street, all because he was wearing a pink suit.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYcf4eOh7Aq/

In a reel that has since gone viral, Bahuguna documented the harassment in real time. As he walked through central London, groups of men shouted comments, hooted, and offered unsolicited commentary. "Welcome to the parade," one voice jeered. Others simply laughed. The women he passed, by contrast, complimented his outfit. "Love your fit," one said. "You look so good," said another.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYcf4eOh7Aq/

"You think, 'This is London, it would be more progressive, more open-minded, more modern,'" Bahuguna reflected in the video. "But clearly not. Every time I pass a group of guys, they make these comments. The girls are lovely. So it's clearly a men problem. Not just grown men — even little kids have walked past me and said absurd sh-t."

## A City's Contradictions

The incident struck a nerve precisely because it shattered a carefully maintained illusion. For many Indians — particularly those in the LGBTQ+ community — London represents an aspirational destination: cosmopolitan, tolerant, a place where you can be yourself. Bahuguna's video is a blunt corrective. Street harassment, particularly against gender-nonconforming individuals, remains a persistent problem across British cities. A 2024 Stonewall survey found that one in five LGBT people in the UK had experienced a hate crime or incident in the preceding year.

For NRIs and diaspora Indians living in the UK, the video resonated on multiple levels. Many shared their own stories of being targeted for how they dress, speak, or express themselves. The assumption that leaving India means escaping prejudice is one that diaspora communities know, from bitter experience, to be false.

## The Industry Rallies

The response from India's creative community was swift and unequivocal. Actor and influencer Kusha Kapila posted a long comment expressing solidarity, adding with characteristic bluntness: "Most men who feel the need to do this have probably never given themselves the freedom to wear beautiful clothes. Deep down, many of them wish they could feel as fabulous as you do." She also pointed out a practical concern familiar to any Indian in London: "Phone neeche rakh please. Pata bhi nahi lagega kab koi chura ke le jaayega."

Actors Shibani Akhtar, Ahsaas Channa, Prajakta Koli, and television star Kavita Kaushik all weighed in with messages of support. Swara Bhasker responded directly to the video, while followers flooded the comments section with messages condemning toxic masculinity and praising Bahuguna's openness.

## Beyond the Reel

Bahuguna, who has over 2 million Instagram followers, has long positioned himself at the intersection of beauty, fashion, and gender discourse. His content — makeup tutorials, styling videos, candid discussions about body image — has made him one of India's most visible male beauty influencers in a space still dominated by rigid expectations of how men should look and behave.

The London incident, however uncomfortable, has amplified a conversation that Bahuguna has been trying to have for years. The fact that it happened not in a small town but on the streets of one of the world's most celebrated cities only underscores the point: homophobia and toxic masculinity are not geographic problems. They are human ones.

For the millions of Indians living abroad — in London, Toronto, Sydney, New York — the video is a reminder that the freedoms promised by Western cities are often incomplete. The pink suit looked fantastic. The men who couldn't handle it had the problem, not the man wearing it.

## What Comes Next

Bahuguna has not indicated whether he plans to file any formal complaint about the harassment. In the UK, homophobic abuse in public spaces can constitute a hate crime under the Public Order Act 1986, though enforcement remains inconsistent.

What the incident has undeniably achieved is visibility. For queer Indians in the diaspora, seeing a prominent creator document and refuse to minimize street harassment is a small but meaningful act of solidarity. Bahuguna wore the suit. He posted the video. And millions watched, shared, and said: enough.
nri_angle: Indian influencer's London experience shatters the myth of Western progressivism for NRI and diaspora communities. The incident resonated with queer Indians abroad who face prejudice in supposedly tolerant cities.
author: Diaspora Desk
